content: During the Great Plague of 1665, the town of Derby in England was severely affected by the bubonic plague, resulting in a significant number of deaths. Certain areas in Derby still bear names that serve as a grim reminder of this tragic period. For instance, Blagreaves Lane was historically known as Black Graves, and Dead Man's Lane is self-explanatory in its reference to the mortality of the time. There is a local legend suggesting that during this period, bodies were buried in an upright position at St. Peter's Church in Derby. However, this claim has been thoroughly investigated and dismissed by experts in the field. Trade during the epidemic was conducted at a designated Market Stone located on Ashbourne Road, which leads into the town center. However, commercial activity nearly came to a halt due to the outbreak, leaving the population at risk of starvation in addition to the deadly threat of plague infection. The Market Stone on Friar Gate, previously known as Nuns Green, was a medieval headless cross. It was also referred to as the Vinegar Stone. This name originated from the practice of placing money into a trough filled with vinegar at the top of the stone. It was believed that the vinegar would act as a disinfectant, sanitizing the coins and thereby preventing the transmission of the plague.
